title: Chunk Recomputation under Real Document Revisions: Measuring Update Cost and Retrieval Quality of Fixed, Recursive, and Content-Defined Chunking
abstract: Chunking strategies for retrieval-augmented generation are almost always evaluated on a static snapshot, yet the documents underlying a knowledge base continue to change. Because chunks are embedded independently, a boundary that moves after an edit forces unchanged text to be re-embedded. We measure this update cost on 120 pairs of adjacent Chinese and English Wikipedia revisions for three stateless chunkers (non-overlapping fixed-size, recursive paragraph-first, and content-defined chunking) under a strict byte-identical reuse rule and a frozen dense encoder. On the 116-article common-success pool, with frozen, length-calibrated parameters, fixed-size chunking recomputes 57-68% of its full new-version embedding-input workload, recursive chunking 38-56%, and content-defined chunking 43-54% (it failed on 4 of 62 Chinese articles), while at these parameters mean evidence recall under a fixed 2048-token retrieval budget differs by less than two percentage points within either language. A cost-only parameter grid shows that the ranking of the two content-aware chunkers changes with chunk-length settings, whereas non-overlapping fixed-size chunking has the highest recomputation cost in every length-matched condition. Controlled edits and a verbatim-presence diagnostic support boundary drift as one contributor to recomputation of text already present in the previous version. Update cost is therefore a substantial, parameter-sensitive dimension that static retrieval evaluations do not expose and that should be reported alongside retrieval quality.

title: Analisis Sentimen Program Magang Generasi Bertalenta Badan Usaha Milik Negara (MAGENTA BUMN) di Media Sosial X Menggunakan Word2Vec dan Support Vector Machine (SVM)
abstract: The State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs) Talent Generation Internship Program (Magenta BUMN) is a human resource development program managed by the Indonesian Human Capital Forum (FHCI) that has attracted considerable public attention on the social media platform X. The high volume of unstructured public opinions makes manual program evaluation challenging. This study aims to measure the model's accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score; evaluate the effectiveness of combining the Word2Vec Skip-gram architecture with a Linear-kernel Support Vector Machine (SVM) to classify public sentiment toward Magenta BUMN; and identify the dominant aspects of positive and negative sentiment. The dataset consists of 664 Indonesian-language tweets collected between January 2023 and November 2025. The data underwent six preprocessing stages and were evaluated using 18 parameter combinations involving variations in data-splitting ratios, vector size, and window size. The best performance was achieved with an 80:20 data-splitting ratio, a vector size of 300, and a window size of 7, yielding an accuracy of 80.45%, precision of 78.46%, recall of 80.95%, and an F1-score of 79.69%. The average cosine similarity of 0.8991 indicates that the model effectively captures contextual relationships between words within the Magenta BUMN domain. Positive sentiment is predominantly associated with career development and financial compensation, whereas negative sentiment primarily concerns selection transparency and technical issues with the platform.

title: Mostly Reading: What Open-Book Scores Measure in Document-Level LoRA Adapters
abstract: Single-document LoRA adapters have been proposed as units of knowledge to be merged and retrieved; yet open-book scoring, with the document in the prompt, can credit a document's own adapter (its specialist) for reading that document as readily as for holding it. Training one adapter for each of 150 Wikipedia articles on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we find that open-book scores mostly measure a reading behaviour every adapter shares: a random adapter trained on another document recovers 82 % of the specialist's open-book advantage over the base model but only 2 % of its advantage on a cloze probe that asks for the same document's facts without providing the source text, a share we cannot distinguish from zero. Content does reach the weights, since the specialists beat the base model in cloze recall by 0.094, and the geometry of their updates follows the documents they read; yet, in a test of 30 queries, adapters chosen by weight-space proximity or text embedding are not distinguishable from random ones on either probe, although that test cannot exclude an advantage of about four fifths of what a query's own adapter gains over a random one. At 16 documents or more, correctly scaled merges recover 87 % to 89 % of the specialists' open-book advantage but only 12 % to 16 % of their cloze advantage, with intervals that run from below zero to at most 32 %, against 94 % for joint training.We also report four silent errors, each of which produced a clean, wrong result.

title: XALIGN: A Human-centric Visual Analytics Approach to Understanding AI Explanations
abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) methods are usually evaluated for technical properties such as faithfulness and robustness. In high-stakes application domains, experts also need to check model predictions against established knowledge. Different explanation methods often disagree, and this disagreement is hard to see when each method is inspected separately. We propose XALIGN, a visual analytics workflow and interface that shows rule-based explanations and several feature attribution methods (TreeSHAP, KernelSHAP, and LIME) side by side for the same Random Forest model. Agreements and contradictions between the methods become visible signals that users can explore and compare with domain knowledge. We apply XALIGN in two case studies: the German Credit dataset and a meteorological dataset, in which events derived from ICON model output and Cloudnet observations are classified. In both, the views reveal discrepancies between the rule-based explanation and the attribution methods that a single method would not show. In an expert evaluation with three specialists, participants found XALIGN useful for identifying influential features and for avoiding over-trust in predictions. Linking rules to attributions was harder for the participant without an XAI background.

title: Agent Behavior Reverse Engineering
abstract: Agent behavior reverse engineering asks what an agent has done, based on theactions it has taken. In its simplest form, the answer is an instruction or promptthat describes the task carried out by those actions. The usual direction is to givean agent a task and let it act; here, the direction is reversed, from actions back to atask. This paper argues that this problem deserves attention as a research direction.It also extends the idea to multi-agent systems, where the aim is to understandwhat each agent did and what they accomplished together. The main motivation issafety: understanding actual behavior can help determine whether an agent carriedout a harmful task. For hypothetical future agents with self-awareness, this abilitycould also help people understand the activities those agents choose for themselvesand their consequences. This paper explains the idea, gives simple examples, andoutlines ways to begin studying it.

title: Multi-Tool Selection for Robotic Systems: Comparing Semantic Retrieval and LLM
abstract: Natural-language interfaces allow users to command robotic systems without interacting directly with mission planners or robotics middleware. Their reliable use depends on robot tool routing, defined here as the selection of the smallest complete subset of predefined executable capabilities required to satisfy a request. This task is particularly difficult for compound instructions, where incomplete selection may omit necessary sensing or monitoring capabilities, while excessive selection may expose irrelevant tools. We compare four routing strategies: three progressively refined ChromaDB-based methods - fixed-threshold retrieval, relative-distance retrieval, and clause-aware aggregated retrieval - and a cloud-hosted 120-billion-parameter language-model baseline. The methods are evaluated on 164 manually annotated prompts organised into three complexity levels, from direct single-tool requests to compound requests requiring at least three tools. Using exact-match accuracy, completeness, precision, a completeness-weighted composite score, and routing latency, CDB-v3 achieves the best macro-average score among the retrieval-only methods, with 0.7822, compared with 0.8869 for the large-model baseline. Although the LLM provides higher routing quality, CDB-v3 exhibits substantially lower latency and can be deployed locally without requiring cloud connectivity. These results identify a quality-latency trade-off between direct large-model selection and clause-aware semantic retrieval for privacy-sensitive, connectivity-constrained, and resource-constrained robotic systems.

title: Generative AI and Copyrightability in the United States: Human Authorship, Creative Control, and AI-Assisted Works
abstract: The U.S. Copyright Office has released its report Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability. This paper explores the copyrightability of AI-generated and AI-assisted works in the United States, focusing on that report and on the jurisprudence of human authorship. It examines the constitutional and statutory bases of human authorship, the importance of Burrow-Giles, Feist, Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid and Thaler v. Perlmutter, and how the Copyright Office has dealt with prompting, human-authored inputs, selection, arrangement, modification and the assistive use of AI. The paper shows that the United States has adopted a case-by-case approach: the use of AI as a tool does not defeat protection, but copyright extends only to expression created by a human author and not to material generated by AI itself. Under current technology, prompts alone do not generally provide sufficient control, but human expression that is perceptible in the output, creative selection and arrangement, and meaningful modification can be protected. The paper sets out the strengths and weaknesses of this approach and suggests more explicit registration, evidentiary and guidance practices, while maintaining the human-authorship requirement.

title: Evaluating Artificial Wisdom (AW): A Trajectory-Based Framework for Context-Sensitive Decision Regulation
abstract: Capability benchmarks measure what large language models can do, but not whether their recommendations remain appropriate as decision conditions change. This paper proposes a trajectory-based measurement framework and prospective validation protocol for artificial wisdom, defined behaviorally as context-sensitive regulation of judgment. Versioned reference specifications determine admissible responses and transition materiality before evaluation. Seven stage-level criteria assess judgment under current conditions, while two transition components assess material-update adequacy and commitment-preserving stability. Stability requires prior adequacy; switching within registered commitment classes is permitted, and persistent error earns no stability credit. A nine-component profile is primary, with a secondary bottleneck score and separate critical-failure reporting. Three simplified simulations examine precision, bottleneck estimation, and sensitivity to model-family count. A single-criterion simulation met its precision criteria at 24 scenarios per domain. Near a bottleneck tie, the estimated minimum had a downward bias of 0.55 points at that size. A simplified incremental-prediction simulation detected a Brier improvement of 0.027 with probabilities of .508 and .742 using eight and twelve families, respectively; it does not establish power for the operational protocol. An exploratory predecessor-rubric study comprising 71 evaluation records illustrates aggregation sensitivity but does not validate the proposed instrument. The twelve-family target remains provisional pending feasibility assessment and calibration of the complete analysis. Whether the profile predicts independent decision outcomes beyond capability remains an open empirical question.

evidence.title: Evaluating Artificial Wisdom (AW): A Trajectory-Based Framework for Context-Sensitive Decision Regulation
evidence.abstract: Capability benchmarks measure what large language models can do, but not whether their recommendations remain appropriate as decision conditions change. This paper proposes a trajectory-based measurement framework and prospective validation protocol for artificial wisdom, defined behaviorally as context-sensitive regulation of judgment. Versioned reference specifications determine admissible responses and transition materiality before evaluation. Seven stage-level criteria assess judgment under current conditions, while two transition components assess material-update adequacy and commitment-preserving stability. Stability requires prior adequacy; switching within registered commitment classes is permitted, and persistent error earns no stability credit. A nine-component profile is primary, with a secondary bottleneck score and separate critical-failure reporting. Three simplified simulations examine precision, bottleneck estimation, and sensitivity to model-family count. A single-criterion simulation met its precision criteria at 24 scenarios per domain. Near a bottleneck tie, the estimated minimum had a downward bias of 0.55 points at that size. A simplified incremental-prediction simulation detected a Brier improvement of 0.027 with probabilities of .508 and .742 using eight and twelve families, respectively; it does not establish power for the operational protocol. An exploratory predecessor-rubric study comprising 71 evaluation records illustrates aggregation sensitivity but does not validate the proposed instrument. The twelve-family target remains provisional pending feasibility assessment and calibration of the complete analysis. Whether the profile predicts independent decision outcomes beyond capability remains an open empirical question.

title: De-identification of child protection intake reports using relationship-based replacement (DI-REBAR)
abstract: Background Child protection contacts are documented in the form of child protection intake reports detailing the child(ren) suspected to be at risk of harm, the notifier's concerns, the alleged person responsible, and other details. These narrative reports remain untapped for statistical reporting and research purposes due to being text-based as well as containing extremely sensitive content. Applying a contextual de-identification approach to child protection narratives opens up the possibility of large-scale automated analysis by external researchers while preserving data privacy and relational meaning. Data 10,000 randomly selected South Australian Department for Child Protection intake reports were provided for this study. A total of 300 (200 development, 100 evaluation) were randomly selected, manually reviewed and annotated. Methods We designed and implemented a context-preserving de-identification pipeline called De-Identification via Relationship-Based Replacement (DI-REBAR) on 10,000 reports while preserving the noted relationships between named individuals. A total of seven indirect identifiers (date, time, school, early learning centre, hospital, prison, sensitive reference numbers) and three direct identifiers (name, address, phone number) were selected for de-identification. A relationship table was temporarily created to map individuals and their relationship to the child of interest, with direct identifiers replaced. Indirect identifiers were replaced by list-based replacement and regular expressions. Results DI-REBAR evaluation showed promising results in macro precision (>0.98), recall (>0.88), and F1-Score (>0.92) across nine out of the ten identifier classes (prison excluded). Each identifier had a range of precision (0.74-1.00), recall (0.61-1.00), and F1-Score (0.66-1.00). Address, phone number, and date have the best performances (>0.98) across precision, recall, and F1-Score. Conclusion This is the first Australian study to automatically de-identify sensitive child protection data whilst preserving relationship information, allowing large-scale text analysis by external researchers in a data custodian's controlled environment. This approach can be applied to other areas that rely on unstructured data such as court documents and police reports. However, human reviewers are still needed to ensure identifiable information is not disclosed.

title: Revisiting Distribution Matching for State-to-Vision Policy Distillation in Laparoscopic Robotic Manipulation
abstract: End-to-end control policies trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL) have emerged as an alternative to conventional surgical robotic control approaches, with recent studies exploring state-based policies trained on privileged state observations. However, such approaches rely on precise physical states that are difficult to obtain reliably in surgical environments. Vision-based RL provides an alternative by learning manipulation policies directly from RGB observations, avoiding explicit state estimation and manually engineered perception pipelines while enabling policies to acquire task-relevant visual representations. Nevertheless, obtaining vision-based policies via pure RL methods for surgical manipulation remains challenging. Thus, imitation learning (IL) becomes another solution, yet it requires a large number of expert demonstrations, which are difficult to obtain in minimally invasive surgery. In this work, we propose a framework for state-to-vision policy distillation in laparoscopic robotic manipulation. Specifically, a state-based policy with privileged observations is employed as the teacher, and a vision-based policy learns from RGB observations and robot proprioceptive information, which requires less expert demonstrations than IL and introduces superior performance than RL methods. We conduct extensive experiments on various surgical manipulation tasks in the simulated environment. Experimental results show that, in the context of laparoscopic robotic manipulation, training vision-based policies with general-purpose RL methods is challenging, whereas our proposed state-to-vision policy distillation leads to more consistent and stable performance across tasks.

title: Mitigating Saliency Collapse: Robust Saliency-Aware Long-Text Image-Text Alignment
abstract: Long-text image-text alignment is essential for fine-grained scene understanding, yet existing methods mainly focus on extending context length or improving local alignment. We identify an overlooked failure mode, saliency collapse, where models over-rely on text that features visual prominence while underutilizing non-salient context. Consequently, retrieval performance degrades sharply when salient content is reduced, despite that the non-salient context remains informative. To address this, we propose RoSA, a saliency-aware finetuning framework that decomposes image-text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views, enabling joint learning of prominent and contextual semantics. We propose a modality-independent decomposition strategy to combine object-level visual saliency estimation with LLM-based text decomposition to bridge vision and language. We employ auxiliary objectives to explicitly align these views, ensuring robust representation with both salient and contextual features. RoSA greatly improves long-text retrieval and demonstrates strong robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks. Moreover, our auxiliary objectives are plug-and-play, bringing consistent gains to existing tuning methods. Code and checkpoints are available at: https://github.com/intelligolabs/RoSA

title: A Gaussian Mixture Model for Multiple Instance Learning With Both Bag‐ and Instance‐Level Features
abstract: ABSTRACT The core challenge of multiple instance learning (MIL) is to predict bag‐level labels with partially or completely unobserved instance‐level labels. Most existing methods focus on instance‐level features and ignore commonly available bag‐level covariates. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel Gaussian mixture model (GMM) framework that fuses both bag‐ and instance‐level features. The framework introduces an instance‐level background class to characterize instances weakly related to the target topic. It models the two types of features with separate Gaussian distributions and fuses cross‐level information by combining the bag‐level label distribution with the conditional distribution of instance‐level labels. For parameter estimation, a two‐step strategy is adopted: Bag‐level parameters are obtained in closed form, while instance‐level parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood via the EM algorithm. Numerical simulations verify the consistency of the proposed estimator, and the proposed method achieves substantially higher prediction accuracy than the baseline GMM (using only single‐level features) and classical MIL methods. Experiments on a real‐world government service hotline dataset show that the method achieves an average AUC of 0.8920, markedly outperforming competing methods. These results indicate that fusing dual‐level features and explicitly modelling background patterns can effectively improve bag‐level label prediction.

title: Agri-SCHOLAR: Simulation-Grounded In-Season Rolling Advisories for Agricultural Crops Using LLM-Bounded Optimization
abstract: Existing agricultural advisories to farmers suffer from several limitations: (a) remain largely expert-driven, (b) do not adequately account for in-season weather, and (c) do not scale to individual farms. In this paper, our objective is to close these gaps by developing Agri-SCHOLAR (Simulation-Grounded Crop Harvest Optimization with LLM-Guided In-Season Advisory Rollouts). Agri-SCHOLAR is a rolling, in-season advisory framework that issues, at intervals of every few days or every week, a personalized advisory using the following information: soil and crop properties, observed weather to date, short-range forecast of weather, and a season extrapolation of weather based on historical analogs. The novelty and depth of Agri-SCHOLAR lies in each advisory being produced by a closed-loop system which couples multiple LLM agents with a powerful crop simulator (such as APSIM in our case). The simulator crucially serves as an evaluation oracle. In Agri-SCHOLAR, the LLM agents propose agronomically sound and feasible bounds on actionable parameters and an optimizer searches within those bounds against a multi-objective reward spanning yield, resource utilization, and economic feasibility. We conduct a detailed 11-year analysis of the maize crop in two selected locations of South Asia and show that Agri-SCHOLAR consistently outperforms the region's standard packages of practice and satisfactorily addresses the limitations of existing agricultural advisories.

title: SecLog-Bench: A Scalable Benchmark for Cybersecurity Log Reasoning with Scaffolded Evidence
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for cybersecurity, leading to growing interest in LLM-based automated cybersecurity log analysis. However, current datasets (1) are limited in scale; (2) rely mainly on single-source evidence; and (3) have only binary or multi-class attack labels, without dense annotations of the reasoning process. To address these limitations, SecLog-Bench has three key features. First, we build an extensible simulation platform that covers 29 attack scenarios, supports repeated execution and the integration of new scenarios, and enables scalable generation of cybersecurity logs with attack-stage labels. Second, we use multi-source logs, including audit logs, application logs, and network traffic, to jointly analyze cyber attacks. Third, we annotate each sample with the essential context for cybersecurity log reasoning and a structured step-by-step evidence chain. We evaluate eight mainstream LLMs on this benchmark for post-detection attack-progress reasoning. Results show that, when provided with scaffolded evidence, current LLMs exhibit modest capability in attack-progress reasoning, with the best model achieving only 44.44% accuracy and 45.07% Macro-F1. Their reasoning remains unreliable; i.e., the highest Stage Reasoning F1 (SRF1) score is only 54.87%. Moreover, even correct predictions may be accompanied by flawed reasoning, and reasoning quality is often misaligned with prediction accuracy.

title: Deep learning-based mitotic quantification for objective adjunct for grading of urothelial carcinoma: a multi-institutional validation study
abstract: Abstract Histological grading of urothelial carcinoma is subject to interobserver variability. We evaluated whether artificial intelligence (AI)-based whole-slide mitotic quantification provides an objective adjunct to histological grading. We developed and validated a deep learning-based mitotic detection framework trained on 91,183 patches with 318,893 annotations. A multi-reader crossover study was conducted in internal ( n = 149) and external ( n = 316) cohorts, where three independent pathologists graded cases in unassisted and model-assisted phases. In the combined cohort ( n = 465), AI-derived mitotic count showed high diagnostic accuracy for high-grade carcinoma (area under the curve [AUC] 0.91, 95% CI 0.89–0.94) at a cut-off of 17.5 mitoses per 2 mm². AI assistance significantly improved mean reader AUC from 0.90 to 0.98 in the internal cohort ( p = 0.038). In the external cohort, the mean reader AUC increased from 0.84 to 0.95, although this difference did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.11). AI assistance also significantly reduced interobserver variability (Fleiss’s κ: 0.72 to 0.93 internally; 0.62 to 0.85 externally; both, p < 0.001). AI-based mitotic quantification provides an objective and standardized adjunct to histological grading and reduces interobserver variability. This approach may improve diagnostic accuracy and support clinical decision-making, pending prospective validation.

title: Truthful by Omission: Click Thinning for LLM-Native Advertising
abstract: Generative AI assistants are becoming an advertising medium, embedding sponsored content in their answers. This setting departs from classical position auctions in two ways: an ad's click-through rate depends on the passage that hosts it, and because users stop at their first click, earlier ads take clicks from later ones. This competition for clicks makes truthfulness delicate: a higher bid can reshape the allocation and put a competitor ahead of the bidder, reducing the bidder's clicks. Existing mechanisms either attain a constant fraction of the optimal welfare (advertisers' total click value) but are not known to be truthful, or are truthful but their welfare guarantee degrades as the number of passages grows. We achieve both even when the answer and its editorial order are fixed before bidding. Assuming each ad's click-through rate when reached is known and unaffected by omitting other ads, we give a computationally efficient mechanism that is truthful in expectation and attains at least half the optimal welfare under free reordering. Our key idea, click thinning, omits ads at random, showing earlier ads less often so that each ad's overall click probability no longer depends on the order of the ads. Welfare maximization then reduces to a tractable matching problem, and solving it exactly with VCG-style payments makes truthful bidding optimal in expectation. Characterizing the click probabilities that omission can achieve sharpens the approximation factor from $2$ to $2-(1-δ)^{K-1}$ when at most $K$ ads are shown and each click-through rate is at most $δ$. This factor is the best possible for any order-preserving rule, even one that ignores incentives and computation, so truthfulness and computational efficiency incur no additional worst-case loss.

title: All‐Optical Dual‐Angle Diffractive Neural Networks for 2D Direction‐of‐Arrival Estimation
abstract: ABSTRACT Accurate direction‐of‐arrival (DoA) estimation in real time is essential for stable terahertz (THz) communications. To overcome the limitations of previous diffractive methods that are restricted to 1D sensing or depend on rotation, and to advance their practical deployment, we propose and experimentally validate an all‐optical dual‐angle diffractive neural network (DA‐DNN) capable of simultaneous 2D angular classification. At the heart of our design is a diffractive aperture placed before the neural network as a physical encoder. It converts the phase‐only angular information carried by the incident wave into a complex optical field enriched with amplitude features, thereby producing robust spatial encoding sensitive to angle. The system is modeled using the Rayleigh–Sommerfeld diffraction integral and optimized through end‐to‐end backpropagation. We fabricate a compact, monolithically integrated DA‐DNN device using 3D printing at high resolution and evaluate it through full‐wave simulations and THz experiments that emulate communication environments. The system accurately recognizes 64 angular combinations over a range, providing a passive and scalable optical solution with low latency for THz communications.

title: Padding to k: A Minimum Count in the Schema Makes Open-Weight Models Pad Their Extraction Lists
abstract: Extraction pipelines ask language models for JSON that follows a schema, and the schema can set a minimum number of list entries. We ask what models do when the document holds fewer items than that minimum. Under a preregistered plan, we test eight open-weight models on 558 real documents from nine annotated datasets, with six more models on hosted services as a reference. Three findings stand out. First, models treat the count as a target: a minimum shown in the schema, but not enforced, raises the share of lists longer than the true count from 34.5% to 55.4%. Second, the padding is hard to catch, because most added entries are real text taken from the document; about half of them pass a check that each entry occurs in the source. Third, common fixes help only partly: a line saying fewer items are fine removes the effect on average but misses more true items, a count in prose ("up to k") also raises over-counting, an "N/A" option under an enforced minimum still leaves half the lists padded, and re-asking with the validation error makes padding far more common. We release the code, answer lists and run records at https://github.com/AbhishekBarali/padding-to-k

title: EEG-Captioner: Grounding EEG-to-Language Generation in Fundamental Signal Properties
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-to-language models offer a promising approach for translating complex neural signals into human-readable descriptions. However, generating plausible language does not necessarily demonstrate that a model has learned to interpret the underlying EEG signal. A direct way to assess such interpretation is to probe objectively measurable properties of the signal itself. We therefore construct an EEG-language dataset of 160,781 segments annotated with signal-level question answering (QA) pairs, where each question targets one of five property families and requires a quantitative comparison involving spectral, spatial, temporal, or lateral signal properties. Each segment is also paired with a feature-grounded EEG caption. We further propose a Dual-Domain EEG Encoder that jointly models temporal waveforms and spectral-spatial representations, and introduce EEG-Captioner, a unified EEG-to-language framework trained with both signal-level QA and EEG caption supervision. Experiments show that the proposed encoder achieves the highest overall macro-averaged balanced accuracy (Macro-BA) among the compared EEG encoders, while EEG-Captioner achieves a Macro-BA of 88.81% on signal-level QA and improves caption factual consistency from 82.06% to 83.46% over caption-only language adaptation, demonstrating the complementary benefits of signal-level QA and caption supervision.

title: ColaBench: Evaluating Memory-Guided Knowledge Acquisition in Personal Agents
abstract: Personal agents need to draw on long-term interaction history to retrieve and apply external knowledge suited to a user's current request. Even an answer grounded in relevant documents can be unsuitable when it overlooks the user's circumstances. This creates two connected challenges: using historical conditions to identify the knowledge needed for a new request, and applying that knowledge to the user's situation. Existing benchmarks advance memory recall, personalized retrieval, and memory-guided action, while the joint evaluation of these two challenges remains underexplored. We introduce ColaBench, a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living, with 349 tasks across 10 Profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. Its Evidence Graph connects personal conditions to their disclosures across public interaction sessions, records prior document exposure, and links answer requirements to personal and newly acquired document evidence. We also introduce MemKB, which uses state summaries to inform queries and rule application, and memory-document links to retrieve knowledge associated with the user's history. MemKB achieves 86.25% Accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task. Task-level analysis finds larger gains on tasks integrating information across multiple historical Facts; error analysis further identifies unsupported personal assumptions and rule misapplication as obstacles to using retrieved evidence. ColaBench provides traceable tasks and an evaluation framework for studying how memory guides knowledge acquisition and rule application.

title: Learning global and local representations for generalized category discovery in neurodegenerative diseases
abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved notable success in closed‐set classification of neurodegenerative diseases, but its performance degrades significantly in more realistic open‐set settings, such as discovering rare or novel disease subtypes from unlabeled data that are not seen during training. Purpose This study introduces, to our knowledge, the first framework for generalized category discovery (GCD) in neurodegenerative diseases using MRI. It aims to leverage labeled data from known categories to automatically identify novel categories within unlabeled datasets. Methods We propose a GCD framework integrating semi‐supervised contrastive learning with global‐local representation learning to jointly optimize feature learning. Globally, we enforce consistency between weakly augmented views of the same instance by aligning their similarity relationships with other embeddings in a support queue. Locally, we treat neighborhood embeddings from the support queue as positive pairs for cross‐instance contrastive learning, enhancing fine‐grained discrimination. This dual strategy results in a unified learning objective that is applicable to both labeled and unlabeled data, effectively narrowing the representation gap among semantically similar instances. Results We evaluate our method on a benchmark dataset comprising six neurodegenerative diseases, with over 1500 patient samples. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms representative state‐of‐the‐art methods. Specifically, our method achieves 66.02% Accuracy and 60.59% Normalized Mutual Information on all categories, and 54.53% Accuracy and 16.67% Normalized Mutual Information on novel categories, surpassing existing state‐of‐the‐art methods. Conclusions Our framework underscores the model's robustness and its practical value in discovering new neurodegenerative disease conditions, highlighting its potential for advancing open‐set diagnostic AI.

title: Interpretive Variation and Discourse Structure in Detecting Enthymemes in Controversial Political Discourse
abstract: Enthymemes are arguments that leave a premise or conclusion unstated, and they are a common persuasion device on social media. Because readers must fill in the missing part themselves, they often disagree on whether a text contains one. This paper asks how to detect and evaluate enthymemes when such disagreement is part of the task. On tweets about vaccination and immigration, each labeled by five annotators, F1 stalls around 0.67 for every fine-tuned model we train, regardless of data size, added features or label type. We therefore ask how these models should be evaluated instead, and propose metrics that compare predictions with the full distribution of annotator votes, together with a model that predicts this distribution directly and captures disagreement better at no cost in F1. We then ask what role discourse structure plays. Models learn to rely on explicit argumentative structure: they reliably recognize tweets without an enthymeme but rarely commit on tweets that contain one. Both the models and a discourse parser miss arguments whose links are left implicit and must be inferred by the reader. Finally, we discuss what these blind spots mean for content moderation systems trained on majority labels.

title: Temporal Naive Bayes: an efficient probabilistic framework for real-time maneuver recognition and anomaly monitoring in autonomous driving
abstract: The capacity to anticipate and identify anomalous behavior remains fundamental to the safety and operational reliability of autonomous mobile systems. Yet temporal modeling approaches currently available tend to demand substantial computational resources or intricate parameter tuning, which meaningfully constrains their adoption on resource-limited edge devices. To address this gap, we introduce Temporal Naive Bayes (TNB), a lightweight and highly interpretable extension of the classical Naive Bayes classifier, developed specifically for sequential sensor data. TNB embeds a first-order autoregressive process directly into the feature likelihood estimation, thereby capturing temporal dependencies while incurring minimal computational overhead. The approach is validated across four scenarios of increasing complexity—from idealized synthetic data through to real-time deployment in the CARLA simulator and a real-world smartphone inertial measurement unit (IMU) dataset. Across these settings, TNB proves effective at isolating critical temporal dynamics, outperforming standard baselines in both multiclass maneuver recognition and anomaly detection tasks. An open-source pipeline accompanies this work, illustrating TNB’s practical value as a lightweight, real-time diagnostic tool for autonomous navigation.

title: A Reality Check of Inference-Time Context Augmentation Methods
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often fail to utilise the context given in the input, resulting in hallucinations or a fallback to parametric knowledge. Context augmentation methods aim to improve model performance by modifying the input, from inserting filler tokens that add computational time to adding relevant content such as elaboration of a context during inference. However, these methods have been evaluated in isolation and only by their performance gains, leaving it unclear how they compare and whether they reliably improve performance. In this paper, we present an evaluation framework spanning five methods that differ in how informative the inserted content is and apply them at the sentence level across seven models spanning multiple sizes on three datasets. We find that accuracy gains are not always genuine improvements but undirected perturbations: the methods correct some predictions while breaking others, particularly when the inserted text allows only for more computational time. Our analysis reveals that methods that bring no additional content primarily change model predictions near the decision boundary. Our findings highlight the need to evaluate the reliability of the accuracy gains before adopting them in practice.

title: Personalization, Prediction, and Persuasion
abstract: This chapter discusses the combination of personalization, prediction, and persuasion into a unified system of AI-based child-centric marketing. Its fundamental aspect is the so-called personalized persuasion that automatizes psychological profiling, predictive future behaviours, and persuasive design to create cognitive and emotional reactions. Through synthesis of the literature we discuss how the AI technology uses digital exhaust or traces left by children using educational apps, games and social media to form highly personalized experiences that are at the level of the child developmental stage. On the methodological level, the research investigates the technical processes underlying such tactics by integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) with machine-learning algorithms like Gradient Boosting and the Random Forest to forecast the purchase intentions. This roadmap is part of the theoretical reflection and practical guide to researchers, marketers, and policymakers interested in knowing how an AI-based marketing ecosystem of the next generation will appear.

title: Diagnostic Loss: Asymmetric Supervision for Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Automated radiology report generation requires models to do more than produce fluent clinical narratives: they must explicitly state supported diagnoses while avoiding unsupported ones. However, existing medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) are typically trained with token-level maximum likelihood objectives, which prioritize text agreement over diagnostically critical terms. As a result, models can miss key diagnoses and introduce wrong ones. We identify this as an objective misalignment between conventional language modeling and the asymmetric diagnostic requirements of radiology reporting. To encode these requirements, we introduce Diagnostic Loss (DLoss), a differentiable, architecture-agnostic objective that operates directly on decoder token probabilities. DLoss separately aggregates probability mass over vocabularies associated with diagnoses supported by the reference report and with unsupported alternatives. Using asymmetric pooling across token positions in the report, it encourages supported diagnoses to receive sufficient probability in at least one position while suppressing spurious probability spikes for unsupported diagnoses across all positions during training. The loss can be applied to existing 3D MedVLMs without modifying their vision backbones, language decoders, or inference procedures, and introduces no additional inference-time computation. We train and evaluate DLoss on 50,000 abdominal CT scans across several 3D MedVLM architectures on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution report-generation benchmarks. Across these settings, DLoss improves diagnostic faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance on conventional language-generation metrics, showing the value of asymmetric sequence-level supervision for radiology report generation. The code for DLoss is available at https://github.com/gmum/DLoss.

title: Clinical Artificial Intelligence in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: From Early Detection and Computational Pathology to Precision Oncology
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being developed to analyze radiological, histopathological, molecular, and clinical data across the non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) pathway. This narrative review examines representative applications through August 2026, focusing on intended clinical use, validation, and the evidence required to influence care. Studies were selected purposively for clinical relevance and methodological importance. Imaging models support investigation of nodule detection, malignancy estimation, and future lung cancer risk, although predictive performance does not establish the benefit of changing screening or diagnostic pathways. In computational pathology, models classify tissue, quantify morphological features, and estimate selected molecular alterations. Foundation models extend these capabilities, but their evaluation requires attention to pretraining provenance and independence of downstream testing. Histology-based molecular prediction does not currently justify replacing validated molecular assays; prioritization of testing requires prospective workflow evaluation. Models evaluated in immunotherapy-treated cohorts can predict response or survival, but these associations do not establish differential benefit between treatments. The principal limitations include selected retrospective populations, incomplete assessment of calibration and clinically relevant thresholds, uncertain transportability, and limited evaluation of model-guided care. Evidence should therefore be interpreted at the level of the individual system and intended decision. Prospective evaluation, appropriate comparators, explicit failure procedures, and post-deployment monitoring are required before technical performance can be translated into clinical benefit.

title: LAST-V2X: Language-Driven Adaptive Scenario Synthesis and Testing for Communication-Induced Failures in V2X Safety Applications
abstract: Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication enables connected vehicles to make safety-critical decisions, but delayed, missing, or incorrect information can compromise driving safety. Systematically testing such failures is challenging because traffic interactions, communication conditions, and application responses must be jointly configured to produce meaningful scenarios. This paper presents LAST-V2X, a language-driven, adaptive framework for automated scenario synthesis and safety testing of V2X applications. LAST-V2X leverages large language models (LLMs) to translate natural-language test descriptions into executable scenarios grounded in roadway geometry, V2X communication semantics, and vehicle behavior. The framework integrates physical traffic simulation with spatially aware communication modeling and message-level fault injection to evaluate how information degradation affects vehicle decisions. To establish whether an observed safety failure is caused by communication rather than the underlying traffic conditions, LAST-V2X employs matched executions under degraded and ground-truth information. Furthermore, an execution-guided refinement mechanism combines parameter search and LLM self-reflection to identify ineffective test configurations, improve scenario effectiveness, and produce minimal reproducible failure cases. Experiments across diverse CARLA environments and V2X safety applications demonstrate the framework's ability to generate reliable scenarios, distinguish communication-induced failures from unrelated safety violations, and substantially improve failure discovery through adaptive refinement. These results establish LAST-V2X as a systematic approach to language-driven, causally verified, and adaptive safety testing for connected vehicle systems.

title: GraphCAD: Geometry-Aware Diffusion on Edge-Adjacency Graphs for CAD Generation
abstract: Generative modeling for Computer-Aided Design (CAD) remains fundamentally challenged by the need to capture the intricate interplay between discrete topological connectivity and precise spatial geometry inherent in Boundary Representations (B-reps). Existing generative approaches largely formulate CAD construction as a sequence modeling problem, but consequently lack an explicit topological inductive bias. In this work, we present GraphCAD, a geometry-aware generative framework that centers modeling on the Edge-Adjacency Graph (EAG), a novel graph-based CAD representation tailored for generative tasks. GraphCAD adopts a hybrid graph diffusion formulation to jointly model the discrete and continuous components of EAG and introduces a geometry-aware denoising mechanism that renders node attributes into spatial point sets. These point sets are encoded by an SE(3)-equivariant backbone and fused into the node representations, thereby grounding the generative process in physical geometry. To support this study, we construct EAGBench, a large-scale dataset of engineering CAD models. Extensive experiments show that GraphCAD can generate complex CAD models with more than 50 faces and achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity and distributional alignment compared with sequence-based baselines.

title: The Invisible Handshake
abstract: This chapter aims to examine the role played by artificial intelligence in determining the consumer behaviors and buying patterns of children in a digital environment. The chapter focuses on the mechanisms employed by artificial intelligence in marketing, which include collecting consumer data, tracking consumer behavior, persuasion architecture, artificial influencers, hyper-personalization, the Internet of Toys, and voice assistants. The chapter is also concerned with the psychological and emotional triggers employed by artificial intelligence in marketing to consumers, which include fear of missing out, gamification, and reward-based engagement systems. The chapter is concerned with the ethical issues associated with artificial intelligence marketing to consumers, which include issues related to consumer data privacy, manipulation, transparency, and the lack of regulations. The chapter is also concerned with emerging trends in artificial intelligence marketing to consumers, which include considerations related to marketing ethics

title: Zero-Shot Forecasting of In-Situ Soil Moisture and Temperature with a Time-Series Foundation Model
abstract: Soil moisture and temperature govern plant-water availability and microbial activity, making them key indicators for evaluating land-restoration efforts on degraded landscapes. However, the physical and data-driven models normally used to forecast them both need information that a newly instrumented restoration site does not yet have: hydraulic parameters for the former and months of per-site training data for the latter. We evaluate TimesFM 1, a 500M-parameter time-series foundation model, zero-shot on 15-minute telemetry from 27 sensor stations across three land-management regimes (Control, Treatment, Scald) at a semi-arid restoration site, forecasting 5 cm and 30 cm soil moisture and enclosure temperature at seven lead times from 1 h to 168 h. Using gap-aware rolling-origin evaluation across sensors, we find that TimesFM beats the best rule-based statistical forecasting baselines (persistence, seasonal-naive, or 7-day climatology) by 21-76% at sub-daily lead times but loses by 6-79% beyond a day, a pattern explained by a diurnal-alignment mechanism that holds for both soil-moisture depths and temperature. A CatBoost baseline trained walk-forward on the same origins with full history and weather covariates never wins overall, and we show that its weakness is partly a cold-start effect specific to short deployments. We additionally quantify the inference cost of zero-shot forecasting on commodity CPU hardware. Our results highlight a practical trade-off between zero-shot forecasting capability, predictive performance, and computational efficiency.

title: Quantum Entanglement Generation and Finite-Range Spin Coupling: A Three-Axis Null Test in a Physical-Observation Dual-Axis Model
abstract: We study the generation of quantum entanglement between two spatially separated spins and propose a two-ion experiment to test a finite-range interaction. In a specified quantum realization of the physical–observation dual-axis (PODA) model, a low-energy expansion of a local matter–field action yields a curl-type spin source. Eliminating the quantized field modes to second order produces a cross interaction containing products of the two endpoint spin operators. We derive the resulting entanglement dynamics from an initial product state and give a measurement-based witness applicable to noisy mixed states. For one static bridge-field channel in an unbounded homogeneous background, the trace of the coupling tensor contains a nonzero contribution set by the response length. The corresponding trace vanishes for the free-space, noncontact, quasistatic magnetic dipole interaction. With finite-source contact terms retained, this distinction leads to a direct estimator: the sum of the signed exchange coefficients measured along three common orthogonal quantization axes equals the trace of the same physical coupling tensor.The proposed trapped-ion protocol specifies phase readout, a distance scan, interleaved axis settings, error calibration, and a likelihood for the raw joint counts. Entanglement certification and interaction testing are separate inferences, based on state records and the tensor trace, respectively. We examine angular errors, motion-mediated coupling, boundaries, secular reduction, and readout dynamics, and calculate the sensitivity and acquisition time for five micrometre-scale separations. An unknown constant offset and a residual inverse-cube background substantially weaken the expected constraints. The model, assumptions, derivations, and statistical criteria are given within the paper. The numerical results are conditional design forecasts, not new measurements. Converting a measured interval into constraints on PODA action parameters requires independent matching to the experimental matter and the selected field channel.

title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters
abstract: Many language-model pipelines end in a closed-set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order-sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately. In a three-seed study at 32 million parameters, per-option scoring beats joint scoring on a held-out sample of a 37-benchmark decision suite by 5.8 points of chance-corrected skill at matched optimizer steps and by 2.8 at approximately matched training compute; two external benchmarks agree, though not significantly on their unseen tasks. Crossing reader with initialisation shows that the advantage requires a reranker initialisation, whose query-candidate pair input matches per-option reading; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Per-option scoring needs 5 to 13 times more encoder passes: at most twice the median latency, but more than four times the mean. Of six released joint encoders (17 million to 1 billion parameters), the 68- and 150-million-parameter models exceed a 435-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited System1-Arena tasks and are at least on par with it on the 145 tasks unseen in training. The smallest answers a median request in 14 milliseconds on 16 processor threads, against 728 for the classifier. Reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the joint models' answers (per-option scoring: none). Up to 68 million parameters, they lead their size range on a public leaderboard's private, mainly in-distribution tests.

title: From Data-Driven to Geology-Informed Learning: Geometry-Aware Graph Transformer Learning for Geo-Energy Systems
abstract: Geo-energy systems involve heterogeneous subsurface properties, irregular spatial structures, and complex interactions. Conventional data-driven models either treat observations independently or rely on graph connectivity without explicitly encoding relative geometry, which limits their ability to distinguish spatially different configurations. This study develops a Geometry-Aware Graph Transformer (GAGT) that integrates node attributes, graph structure, and relative geometric information through a learnable geometric bias in the attention mechanism. A controlled synthetic experiment with 300 irregularly distributed three-dimensional nodes compares a multilayer perceptron (MLP), a Graph Transformer (GT), and GAGT under identical settings. Across 10 random seeds, GAGT achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.1569, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.2152, and a coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of 0.8678, reducing MAE and RMSE by 35.77% and 33.95%, respectively, relative to GT. In this controlled setting, explicit geometry therefore carries predictive information that graph connectivity alone does not provide. GAGT can serve as a geometry-aware representation layer between purely data-driven learning and more comprehensive geology-informed modeling; validation with real geological data and physically constrained simulations is still required.

title: Bound-Conditioned Latent Inference for Progressive Image Compression
abstract: Progressive image compression reconstructs images from prefixes of a single bitstream and therefore involves sequential latent inference under partial observations. Existing trit-plane codecs mainly treat decoded trits as discrete symbols for probability prediction, without fully exploiting their role as interval constraints on the underlying continuous latents. We propose bound-conditioned latent inference (BLI), a framework that reformulates progressive trit-plane coding as sequential latent inference under shrinking interval constraints. At each coding step, the trits decoded so far define lower and upper bounds for each latent element. BLI uses the center and width of these bounds, together with hyperprior information shared by the encoder and decoder, to jointly refine the Gaussian parameters $(μ,σ)$ for entropy modeling and the latent estimate $\hat{y}$ for reconstruction. As additional trits are decoded, the feasible intervals shrink monotonically, yielding tighter constraints for the next inference step and enabling flexible in-plane refinement schedules. Experiments on Kodak, CLIC, and JPEG-AI show that BLI achieves state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance among progressive image codecs, reducing BD-rate by $17.78\%$ over DPICT and by $7.96\%$ over CTC on Kodak, while replacing CTC's plane-specific predictors with a shared model that uses about $5.3\times$ fewer parameters and achieves lower latency than CTC.

title: An Integrative Approach for Subtyping Mental Disorders Using Multimodal Data
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding the biological and behavioral heterogeneity underlying psychiatric disorders is critical for advancing precision diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. This paper addresses the scientific question of how multimodal data, which spans clinical, cognitive, and neuroimaging measures, can be integrated to identify biologically meaningful subtypes of mental disorders. We introduce Mixed INtegrative Data Subtyping (MINDS), a Bayesian hierarchical model designed to jointly analyze mixed‐type data for simultaneous dimension reduction and clustering. Using data from the adolescent brain cognitive development (ABCD) Study, MINDS integrates clinical symptoms, cognitive performance, and brain structure measures to subtype attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and obsessive‐compulsive disorder (OCD). Our method leverages Pólya–Gamma augmentation for computational efficiency and robust inference. Simulations demonstrate improved stability and accuracy compared to existing clustering approaches. Application to the ABCD data reveals clinically interpretable subtypes of ADHD and OCD with distinct cognitive and neurodevelopmental profiles. These findings show how integrative multimodal modeling can enhance the reproducibility and clinical relevance of psychiatric subtyping, funding data‐driven policies for early identification and targeted interventions in mental health.

title: Energy and Latency First: How Deployment Constraints Reverse Time-Series Model Selection
abstract: AI models, and time-series models in particular are typically ranked by accuracy and deployed under constraints absent from that ranking. In this paper, we study a real setting where these constraints are explicit and measurable: handover pre- diction in cellular networks, where inference runs on the User Equipment once per 40 ms measurement period and must complete before the network acts. The timing bound is hard: a late prediction is superseded by the measurement it was predicting, while energy is a cumulative budget spent for the life of the device. Neither appears in the objective these models are selected on. We evaluate eight architectures under a protocol that screens for deadline feasibility at the tail rather than the mean, then ranks the feasible models on measured inference energy, count- ing the feature computation that precedes the forward pass and is usually omitted. Gradient-boosted trees on handcrafted temporal features are the most accurate model (F1=0.974) and among the cheapest to run, while the neural architecture an accuracy-only benchmark would rank first (CNN-1D, F1=0.914) costs over 3 times more energy per inference under a realistic duty-cycled deployment pattern. We give three conditions under which this outcome should be expected, so the finding applies beyond telecommunications. Accuracy-only benchmarking does not merely under-report deployment cost. It can rank first a model that cannot be deployed.

title: Characteristic Analysis of Methods to Counteract Adversarial Machine Learning Attacks
abstract: In the era of technological evolution and digital transformation, machine learning and artificial intelligence take a significant part of intelligent systems’ development. Together with the integration of smart and autonomous operations in everyday life, novel security issues arise. One such a malicious threat against the security of machine learning models is the adversarial machine learning (AML) attack. It consists in alteration of the original data samples used to train or test the model with indistinguishably small feature modifications that results in inaccurate processing outcome. In this paper, the most significant strategies to counteract AML attacks are studied and compared through several characteristics that have main influence on their successful implementation in different realization scenarios.

title: ReDence: A Hybrid Agentic and Decision-Model Framework for Rapid, Evidence-Grounded Detection of Modern Social Engineering Scams
abstract: Detecting online social engineering (SE) scams often requires examining website workflows, verifying claims against external sources, and connecting evidence across multiple pages. Existing detectors provide limited support for these investigations, leaving analysts to manually gather and validate evidence, which inevitably delays detection and subsequent takedown of these attacks. To address this gap, we present ReDence, an open-source hybrid framework for adaptive, evidence-grounded detection across diverse SE scam categories. ReDence combines two locally hosted models with complementary responsibilities: a fine-tuned multimodal agentic Investigator (Qwen3.5-4B) that performs investigative planning, evidence interpretation, and reporting, and a specialized Decider (Tev1) that handles binary and multiple-choice tasks, including browser-action selection, evidence assessment, and decisions about whether to continue an investigation. By delegating discrete decisions to a specialized model, ReDence reduces reliance on lengthy language-model responses, while preserving the reasoning capabilities required for complex investigations. Our evaluation demonstrates that ReDence achieves 96\% accuracy in detecting scams across twelve SE scam categories, substantially outperforming existing detectors while being at least four times faster than comparable agentic models without compromising investigative depth. ReDence also produces structured, evidence-grounded reports that document investigative actions, supporting and contradictory evidence, and collected artifacts, which allow analysts to independently audit detection decisions and utilize the collected evidence to support subsequent mitigation and takedown efforts.

title: ANALISIS SENTIMEN KOMENTAR NETIZEN PADA MEDIA SOSIAL INSTAGRAM TIMNAS INDONESIA MENGGUNAKAN METODE NAÏVE BAYES DAN SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINE
abstract: Social media has become an integral part of modern society, providing a platform for public expression. In Indonesia, soccer is a popular sport, and the Indonesian national team is a major topic of discussion on social media, especially Instagram. This study aims to analyze the sentiment of netizen comments on the official Instagram account of the Indonesian national team (@timnasindonesia) using the Naïve Bayes and Support Vector Machine (SVM) methods. The data used consisted of 2,920 comments from 50 posts between September 28, 2023, and May 10, 2024, focusing on the U-23 and Senior National Team matches. Naïve Bayes and SVM were chosen because both are effective methods for sentiment classification. Naïve Bayes uses a probabilistic approach, while SVM seeks the best hyperplane to separate data classes. The results of the study show that both methods can be used to analyze sentiment with a good level of accuracy. Testing results on each training and testing data with different presentations will give different accuracy results. The test results from the Naive Bayes method obtained the highest accuracy value of 69% with a ratio of 70:30. Meanwhile, the Support Vector Machine (SVM) method obtained the highest accuracy of 74% at the same ratio. It can be concluded that the Support Vector Machine method obtained a higher accuracy value than the Naive Bayes method, making it more optimal for use in classifying the sentiment of netizen comments in this study.

title: Once a Tree, Always a Tree? Cross-lingual Transfer of Hierarchical Generalization in Language Models
abstract: Language models (LMs) often exhibit successful cross-lingual transfer through continued (pre)training, still their underlying process remains unclear. One possibility is that LMs can leverage the evidence toward language-universal principles, namely, hierarchical structure, from a source language (L1) to a new language (L2), while many other non-linguistic explanations, e.g., improved initialization of position embeddings, can be potentially possible. In this study, to quantify the cross-linguistic transferability of linguistic evidence in cross-lingual LM training, we introduce a new experimental design, namely, a cross-lingual poverty-of-stimulus (CPOS) setting that ablates how LMs' hierarchical generalization in L2 can be led by structural evidence provided in L1. We contrast counterfactual L1 and L2 learning scenarios where the L2 corpus is ambiguous between linear and hierarchical grammar rules, while the amount of positive evidence for the hierarchical rule is controlled on the L1 side. Our experimental results show that LMs can partially, yet not perfectly, transfer L1 structural evidence to L2, yielding only a small but detectable hierarchical bias, while the strength of transfer depends on language pairs. We further ablate the conditions for successful transfer, motivated by recent reports on the substantial impact of vocabulary overlap. We indeed find that vocabulary overlap is crucial even for the cross-lingual transfer of hierarchical syntactic generalization. This suggests that this also explains the language-pair-dependent tendencies in the main experiments and suggests that the transfer of linguistic evidence in continued new-language learning is only conditionally achievable.

title: Cohort Divergence Does Not Consistently Outperform Single-Rollout Judging for Early Warning of LLM Agent Failure
abstract: Early warning of failure would let costly episodes of large language model (LLM) agents be stopped early. Across five model families and five task domains (3421 usable rollouts), we study a black-box signal: the divergence of a rollout’s judged goal progress from sibling rollouts of the same task after k steps. Under our original judging protocol, cohort divergence predicted failure (pooled AUROC 0.73 in retail). A judge swap revealed that the judge had received a task identifier in place of the task objective. After re-judging with the correct objective, the cohort signal fell to chance in retail and airline (0.47 to 0.52), and a single-rollout judge score had the higher point estimate in eight of ten combinations of domain and horizon. In paired contrasts, before adjustment for multiple comparisons, cohort divergence was significantly worse in two and better in one. Of three pre-specified failure-onset profiles, one met its criterion under the original protocol and none under the corrected one. Task-preserving perturbations produced no detectable amplification of divergence. In an abort simulation, under the stated cost assumptions, the cohort monitor lost tokens for every model, and the judge monitor saved tokens for two of five and had no usable operating point for the other three. Judge instructions are thus a first-order threat to validity in agent-monitoring research.

title: Doubly Robust Distributionally Robust Offline Contextual Pricing
abstract: Offline contextual pricing often relies on logged observational data, but faces challenges from distributional shifts between training and deployment environments. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) provides a principled approach to off-policy evaluation and learning (OPE/L). However, existing methods are mostly limited to discrete actions. Recent work has explored DRO for continuous treatments using inverse propensity weighting (IPW), while such IPW-based estimators can be sensitive to the convergence rate of propensity score estimates, particularly when estimated nonparametrically, which may lead to larger estimation errors and regret. In this work, we develop a doubly robust (DR) framework for distributionally robust OPE/L in continuous pricing settings. For evaluation, we propose a localized DR estimator that addresses the computational challenges of worst-case expectations by fitting only a small number of regressions, comparable to standard non-robust DR, while achieving semiparametric efficiency under mild product rate conditions. For learning, we leverage the inherent smoothness of demand noise to handle pricing-specific discontinuities in revenue outcomes (e.g., threshold-based purchase decisions), establishing a finite-sample regret bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_p(T^{-s/(2s+1)})$ for smoothness orders $s=1,2$. This bound improves upon existing regret rates in existing DRO-based off-policy learning (OPL) for continuous treatments. Extensive experiments under various levels of distribution shift validate our proposed framework.

title: Information Preservation in Communication-Constrained Neural Representation Transfer: Classical and Quantum-Inspired Amplitude Encoding
abstract: Neural representations learned by neural networks encode task-relevant information, but their behavior under communication constraints is still poorly understood. We propose an information-theoretic framework for the comparison of classical compression and quantum-inspired amplitude encoding for the transfer of representations under controlled dimensional constraints. We analyze frozen intermediate features extracted from a pretrained ResNet-50 on the ImageNet-1K validation set at different depths in the network. The classical pipeline performs rate-controlled dimensionality reduction and uniform quantization, while the quantum-inspired pipeline does amplitude encoding and computational-basis probability decoding without variational circuits or trainable quantum parameters. Quality of representation was evaluated using differential entropy and a decoder-based lower bound on mutual information. Classical compression achieves higher decoder-based mutual information lower bounds at moderate and high communication budgets. However, the quantum-inspired pipeline retained a larger fraction of decoder-extractable task-relevant information under severe dimensional compression, with resource-normalized information efficiency providing a complementary perspective to the substantially higher absolute decoder-based mutual information lower bounds of the classical pipeline. Robustness analyses with qubit reduction and physically motivated noise models showed predictable degradation. Ablation and SHAP analyses indicate that task-relevant information is structured within representational subspaces. These findings support quantum-inspired representation transfer as a framework for studying communication-efficient neural representation transfer under low-bandwidth constraints.

title: Ground-Truth-First Benchmarking of Reinforcement Learning via Converse Optimality: From Smooth, Fully Observed Systems to Non-Smooth or Partially Observed Tasks
abstract: Benchmarking in reinforcement learning is usually relative: algorithms are ranked by returns on environments with unknown optima. Distance to optimality remains unobservable, while conclusions may depend on reward design, stochasticity, hyperparameters, environment selection, and simulator details. We develop a ground-truth-first framework based on converse optimality, constructing each task with a certified optimal value function and policy withheld from learners and used only for evaluation. The framework unifies two modes: sensitivity benchmarking samples certified environments from continuous-time generators to assess robustness to task variation, while oracle-referenced comparison uses native discrete-time generators to evaluate policies via optimality gap, regret, and policy error. Continuous-time models support physically interpretable sensitivity studies but introduce dependence on the simulator step ($Δt$) and numerical scheme. title: Explainable AI Based Interpretation With Big Data Analytics for Healthcare Industry—A Review
abstract: ABSTRACT Big data analytics plays a crucial role in providing usable insights for improving the strategic planning of the diagnosis methods in the healthcare industry, and here the big data helps the clinical professionals analyze the large numbers of datasets obtained from different demographic groups to identify which factor is blocking the patients from taking up their treatment. Despite the benefits guided by the information age, healthcare technologies encounter difficulties such as data protection, loss, and management issues. Artificial intelligence (AI) has helped more in the adaptation and handled the pandemic situations. However, the realization of AI's potential in healthcare is tempered by concerns regarding the trustworthiness and explaining ability of AI systems. ML algorithms have shown promise in detecting and managing healthcare complications, while the deployment of critical medical Internet of Things applications necessitates efficient mechanisms to address patient privacy concerns. Furthermore, the use of AI and machine learning (ML) in healthcare enables disease outbreak prediction, highlighting the versatility of AI in the health sector. However, there are still obstacles to achieving interpretability and accuracy in AI systems. Given these challenges, explainable AI (XAI) methods that are technically capable, ethically responsible, and meet the needs of healthcare practitioners are increasingly important. This review sky‐scrapes the importance of transparency, effective data management, human oversight, and international collaboration in advancing XAI in healthcare. Ultimately, the paper calls for the generalization of XAI frameworks and the prioritization of interpretation, data privacy, and security for future research, which has the full potential of XAI in revolutionizing healthcare.

title: Measuring the Reasoning-Action Coupling in Driving Vision-Language-Action Models through Counterfactuals
abstract: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models bring an appealing form of explainability to a safety-critical domain, since a system that can state the reasons for its maneuvers offers the transparency that deployment and public trust in autonomous driving demand. These models read the world into language before they act on it, describing the scene and reasoning over it in text that ranges from chain-of-thought to multi-stage question answering on the way to a trajectory. That framing quietly assumes two separable properties, namely that the trajectory follows the generated reasoning and that the generated reasoning tracks the causes that actually produce the trajectory. To thoroughly investigate these properties, we apply causal, counterfactual interventions to four driving VLAs across different benchmarks. First, we perturb the models' own reasoning and show that altering its meaning produces small trajectory changes relative to blanking the same models' camera inputs, a pattern that persists across benchmarks and model architectures. We then construct scene-level counterfactuals through photorealistic removal of key objects named in the models' reasoning and analyze whether the generated reasoning and trajectories track these changes. Overall, our findings indicate that the reasoning these models present to account for their resulting driving behavior is weakly coupled to that behavior itself, pointing to limits on the explainability these systems are intended to provide.

title: FedSTIP-Tuning: Federated Black-Box Prompt Tuning with Aggregate-Only Feedback and Common-Candidate Optimization
abstract: Federated black-box prompt tuning enables organizations to adapt a proprietary frozen language model without centralizing their labeled data, but local search-state aggregation does not directly define a shared pooled-data objective, and client-specific feedback can expose private signals. We propose FedSTIP-Tuning, which composes a three-party permutation-based protected forward propagation with a common-candidate population and pairwise-masked loss aggregation in a cross-silo setting. All participating clients evaluate the same prompt candidates, and the coordinator ranks their sample-weighted aggregate losses, thereby optimizing the empirical objective over the fixed union of client shards under full participation. Under the stated semi-honest and non-collusion assumptions, the aggregation layer hides each released loss vector’s client-level decomposition, while the aggregate values and execution metadata remain observable to their authorized parties. On RoBERTa-large, FedSTIP-Tuning exceeds the strongest evaluated FedBPT configuration by 6.40, 2.66, and 7.60 percentage points on AG News, SST-2, and DBpedia, respectively, under matched forward budgets. Its protected forward preserves all candidate rankings across 600 paired generations and is 861× and 957× faster than a generic interactive two-party computation reference on the RoBERTa-base warm and cold paths, and 694× and 578× on RoBERTa-large.
